messages.subject: priors for model with categorical_logit
parts:
Hi, I'm using categorical_logit with k-1 approach (I think that's the name at least). I would like
to add more or less informative priors so that the model "knows" that one choice is much more likely than the others. But I'm not sure how to indicate that with the logit approach, if I were using categorical(), I guess the solution would be to use a dirichlet as a prior, but with the logit, I would need to "unsoftmax" the output of the dirichlet, because I want to add an effect for conditions on top of the output of the dirichlet (in the more complex version also hierarchical structure). I'm posting a simplified version of my model. I hope I'm clear, but basically, in the version I'm posting, it's A[1] which should be much larger than the A[2:]. And I have no clue on how to indicate that.

Thanks!


data {
  int<lower=0> N_obs;
  int winner[N_obs]; #choice that was selected
  int N_choices;
  vector[N_obs] cond;


}
parameters {
  vector[N_choices-1] A;
   vector[N_choices-1] beta;
 
}


transformed parameters {
  vector[N_choices] B;
  B[1:N_choices-1] <- A;
  B[N_choices] <- 0;
}


model {
  beta ~ normal(0,1);
  A ~ normal(0,2);
  for(i in 1:N_obs) winner[i] ~  categorical_logit(B +  beta *cond[i]);
}


generated quantities {
vector[N_choices] P;
P <- softmax(B);
}

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] priors for model with categorical_logit
parts:
> On Mar 22, 2016, at 9:50 AM, Bruno Nicenboim <bruno.n...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
>
> Hi, I'm using categorical_logit with k-1 approach (I think that's the name at least). I would like
> to add more or less informative priors so that the model "knows" that one choice is much more likely than the others.

I think the confusion's coming in because a prior is a density
over parameters, not over outcomes. That is, we write

y ~ normal(mu, sigma);

mu ~ ... prior on mu ...

sigma ~ ... prior on sigma ...

we don't put a "prior" on y, because it's the outcome. Our prior
has to be on mu and sigma if we have a normal likelihood.

Some comments below. That program won't compile, by the way.

> But I'm not sure how to indicate that with the logit approach, if I were using categorical(), I guess the solution would be to use a dirichlet as a prior, but with the logit, I would need to "unsoftmax" the output of the dirichlet, because I want to add an effect for conditions on top of the output of the dirichlet (in the more complex version also hierarchical structure). I'm posting a simplified version of my model. I hope I'm clear, but basically, in the version I'm posting, it's A[1] which should be much larger than the A[2:]. And I have no clue on how to indicate that.
>
> Thanks!
>
>
> data {
> int<lower=0> N_obs;
> int winner[N_obs]; #choice that was selected
> int N_choices;
> vector[N_obs] cond;
>
>
> }
> parameters {
> vector[N_choices-1] A;
> vector[N_choices-1] beta;
>
> }
>
>
> transformed parameters {
> vector[N_choices] B;
> B[1:N_choices-1] <- A;
> B[N_choices] <- 0;
> }
>
>
> model {
> beta ~ normal(0,1);
> A ~ normal(0,2);
> for(i in 1:N_obs) winner[i] ~ categorical_logit(B + beta *cond[i]);
> }

Here B is your intercept. You want to put the prior on B. But
with the K-1 parameterization, you have to do that knowing that
one value is fixed. That's why we say the K-parameterization is easier
to deal with for priors because of the symmetry.

>
>
> generated quantities {
> vector[N_choices] P;
> P <- softmax(B);
> }

Why would you care about softmax(B)? That's just giving you
the posterior predictive where cond == 0.

- Bob

  for(i in 1:N_obs) {

And yes, I don't want to put a prior on the outcome, I know the prior in this model should be on "A" (which I then feed in B). But I might have not been clear. So if I stick to the K-1, do I have a way to indicate that softmax(B)[1] should be around .7?  Or that it should be 3-5 times larger than the other softmax(B)[2:]?

And how bad is to use the K parametrization? And even if I use it I still don't know how to indicate what I want. If I had 2 choices, I know that .9 in log-odds scale should represent 70%. But I'm really lost since I have more choices, and the value of one choice in the transformed scale affects the rest of the choices.
 
I hope I'm more clear now

Bests,

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] priors for model with categorical_logit
parts:
> On Mar 22, 2016, at 4:52 PM, Bruno Nicenboim <bruno.n...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Thanks for the fast answer, and sorry, I oversimplified the model for loop should be:
>
> for(i in 1:N_obs) {
> vector[N_choices] effect;
>
> effect[1:N_choices-1] <- beta *cond[i];
> effect[N_choices] <- 0;
> winner[i] ~ categorical_logit(B + effect );
> }
>
>
> softmax(B) should indicate the "underlying" probability of the choices, isn't it?

I don't know what that means. It's the log-odds when the cond variables
are all zero.

> What I want to achieve is to inform the model that the choice 1 is much more likely than the others (regardless of the actual data that I'm seeing).
>
> And yes, I don't want to put a prior on the outcome, I know the prior in this model should be on "A" (which I then feed in B).

I don't see an A any more. Any prior you want here toward one category
or the other should be built into B. But if you have the regression
beta * cond[i], then you can't control that directly.
> But I might have not been clear. So I understood that the K-1 parametrization is "better" than the K.

Only in the sense of being well identified without a prior,
which can help with computation.
> So if I stick to the K-1, do I have a way to indicate that softmax(B)[1] should be around .7? Or that it should be 3-5 times larger than the other softmax(B)[2:]?

B = (A[1], ...A[K-1], 0).

With K outcomes, you can't control the dimensions independently. You can make
softmax(B)[1] near 0.7 when you know all the other values of B are
near zero, but otherwise, you only know the log odds relative to the
fixed value.
> And how bad is to use the K parametrization?
Not that bad if you have priors.

> And even if I use it I still don't know how to indicate what I want. If I had 2 choices, I know that .9 in log-odds scale should represent 70%. But I'm really lost since I have more choices, and the value of one choice in the transformed scale affects the rest of the choices.

But anyway, you probably don't want all of this hand-tweaked
coaxing of solutions. Put some reasonable priors on the parameters
and let the data decide what the answer should be.

- Bob
